Possible imprecision: the text says TextVectorization "includes a \"[PAD]\" at index zero of the learned vocabulary". In Keras, index 0 is the padding/mask index, but get_vocabulary() lists it as the empty string "" rather than the literal token "[PAD]" (index 1 is "[UNK]"). The concept is right; the printed token name is a convention. The notes explain this.

overview.title: Sequence models: why, which architectures, and padding/truncation
overview.main_topic: Moving from hand-engineered n-gram features to models that learn from the raw token sequence, and preparing fixed-length integer sequences with [PAD] padding and truncation to 600 tokens
overview.central_idea: Instead of manually engineering order features (n-grams), expose the model to the full token sequence and let it learn positional dependencies. Sequence models (RNNs, 1D ConvNets, Transformers) need rectangular batches, so variable-length reviews are padded with a special [PAD] token or truncated; for IMDb, truncating at 600 words keeps 95% of reviews whole.
overview.importance: It opens section 14.5 and sets up the data format (integer sequences of shape (batch, 600)) used for all sequence models in the rest of chapter 14 and for the Transformer in chapter 15.
learning_objectives: Explain why n-gram feature engineering does not scale and what sequence models do instead
Name the three architecture families for sequence models mentioned in the book
Explain why batches must be rectangular and how padding and truncation achieve this
Pad and truncate a pair of example sentences to length 8
Justify the 600-token truncation length using the IMDb length statistics
prerequisites: Bigram model and the limits of n-grams (p.427-428)
Tokenization into integer IDs and the [UNK] token (p.409-411)

summary:
Section 14.5 begins by drawing the lesson of the last two models: **sequence information matters**. The bigram model improved on the bag-of-words model with features carrying some local word order. But those features were **manually engineered** and only scale to the order of a few neighbouring words (p.428). In the usual deep learning spirit, the better approach is to **expose the model to the raw word sequence** and let it **learn positional dependencies** between tokens itself.

Models that take the full token sequence are **sequence models**. Three architecture choices are listed: an **RNN**, as for timeseries in the previous chapter; a **1D ConvNet**, like the image models but convolving over one sequence dimension; and a **Transformer**, the subject of the next chapter.

All of them need inputs preprocessed into **ordered integer sequences of token IDs**, with one extra wrinkle: batched GPU computation requires **rectangular** inputs, but reviews vary from a few sentences to several paragraphs. The fix is to **truncate** long sequences and **pad** short ones with a special `"[PAD]"` token, analogous to `"[UNK]"`. With a target length of 8, "the quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog" is truncated to its first eight tokens (dropping "dog"), and "the slow brown badger" gets four `[PAD]`s. Padding speeds up batch computation, but care is needed so that **padding tokens don't affect predictions**.

For IMDb the authors **truncate at 600 words**: the average review has 233 words and only 5% are longer than 600. The vectorization layer (named `Vectorization` in the text; it is `TextVectorization`) can pad or truncate and reserves index 0 of its vocabulary for padding. The code follows on p.430.

paragraphs.excerpt: Our last two models indicated that sequence information is important.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The two set models showed that sequence information matters: adding features with some local word order improved a basic linear model.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The 88% -> 90% gain from unigrams to bigrams (p.426, p.428) is evidence that word order carries signal for sentiment.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the empirical motivation for sequence models.
connections: p.428: the bigram model reaches 0.90116 test accuracy versus 0.88388 for bag-of-words

paragraphs.excerpt: However, this was done by manually engineering input features, and we can see
paragraphs.what_it_says: The order information was added by manually engineering features, an approach that only scales to the ordering of a few words. As is often the case in deep learning, instead of building such features ourselves, we should expose the model to the raw word sequence and let it learn positional dependencies between tokens.
paragraphs.what_it_means: n-grams are hand-designed features with an exponential cost in n (p.428). A deep model can learn which order patterns matter, at any distance its architecture allows, from the raw data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This repeats a central theme of the book: deep learning replaces feature engineering with learned representations.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: a sequence model computes a function of the ordered tokens $f(t_1, \dots, t_L)$ whose order sensitivity is learned through shared parameters (recurrent weights, convolution kernels, attention), instead of a separate weight per explicit phrase.

terminology.meaning: Manually designing input features (such as n-grams) instead of letting the model learn representations.
Relationships between tokens that depend on their order and relative positions.

connections: p.428: n-grams beyond trigrams become intractable

paragraphs.excerpt: Models that ingest a complete token sequence are called, simply enough, sequence models.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Models that take the complete token sequence are called sequence models. There are a few architecture choices: an RNN as for timeseries, a 1D ConvNet convolving filters over the single sequence dimension, or a Transformer (next chapter).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The three families differ in how they mix information across positions. RNNs process tokens in order and carry a state. 1D ConvNets apply learned filters to local windows (like learned n-gram detectors). Transformers use attention to connect any pair of positions directly.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames the rest of chapter 14 (an LSTM on p.430) and chapter 15 (the Transformer).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: a 1D convolution with kernel size k over token vectors is like a learned, soft k-gram detector whose weights are shared across positions. This links it directly to the n-gram idea, but without an explicit phrase vocabulary.

terminology.meaning: A model whose input is the full ordered token sequence.
A convolutional network whose filters slide along a single (sequence) axis.
An attention-based architecture covered in the next chapter.

paragraphs.excerpt: Before taking on any of these approaches, we must preprocess our inputs into ordered sequences.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Inputs must become ordered integer sequences of token IDs, as in the tokenization part of the chapter, with one wrinkle: batch computations need rectangular inputs so they can be parallelized across the batch on a GPU, but tokenized inputs almost always vary in length; IMDb reviews range from a few sentences to multiple paragraphs.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A batch is a single tensor of shape (batch_size, sequence_length). A tensor can't have rows of different lengths, so all reviews in a batch must be brought to the same length before stacking.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This constraint shapes all sequence preprocessing, here and in later chapters.

terminology.meaning: A batch tensor in which every sample has the same shape, allowing parallel computation.

connections: p.409: tokenizing text into a sequence of integer IDs

paragraphs.excerpt: To accommodate this fact, we can truncate our input sequences or “pad” them
paragraphs.what_it_says: Sequences can be truncated, or padded with a special token "[PAD]", similar to the "[UNK]" token. For a desired length of eight, two example sentences are tokenized as shown in the following code blocks.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Padding adds filler tokens at the end of short sequences; truncation cuts long ones. The 9-word "the quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog" loses "dog"; the 4-word "the slow brown badger" gets four [PAD] tokens.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It introduces the second special token after [UNK] and the fixed-length convention used in listing 14.19.

terminology.meaning: Special filler token used to extend short sequences to a fixed length; conventionally index 0.
Cutting a sequence down to a maximum length.

connections: p.410: the [UNK] token for out-of-vocabulary words

paragraphs.excerpt: This will allow our batch computation to proceed much faster, although we will need
paragraphs.what_it_says: Padding lets batch computation proceed much faster, but we must be careful that padding tokens don't affect the quality of predictions.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A model that reads [PAD] tokens as real input could be misled. For example, an RNN that reads hundreds of trailing pads after a short review may partly "forget" the review. Techniques such as masking (telling layers to skip pad positions) address this.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It foreshadows padding-related problems and the masking solution in the following pages.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not on this page): Keras supports masking, for example via Embedding(mask_zero=True), so that downstream layers ignore index-0 positions.

terminology.meaning: Marking padded positions so that layers ignore them (beyond this page).

paragraphs.excerpt: To keep a manageable input size, we can truncate our IMDb reviews after
paragraphs.what_it_says: Reviews are truncated after the first 600 words, which is reasonable because the average review is 233 words and only 5% exceed 600. The vectorization layer (printed as `Vectorization`) has an option for padding or truncating and includes "[PAD]" at index zero of the learned vocabulary.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 600 is a trade-off: long enough to keep 95% of reviews intact, short enough that batches of shape (32, 600) are manageable. Most reviews will be heavily padded, since a 233-word review is followed by about 367 pad positions. Index 0 is reserved for padding, so a 0 in the sequence means "no token here".
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It fixes output_sequence_length=600 for listing 14.19 (p.430) and explains the trailing zeros in the batch shown there.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): in Keras, TextVectorization's get_vocabulary() shows index 0 as the empty string "" (the padding/mask value) and index 1 as "[UNK]". The layer pads with zeros at the end and truncates from the end.

terminology.meaning: TextVectorization argument that pads or truncates every output sequence to a fixed length (used on p.430).

connections: p.430: listing 14.19 uses max_length = 600 and output_mode="int"

concepts.name: Sequence model
concepts.definition: A model that ingests the complete, ordered token sequence and learns positional dependencies between tokens.
concepts.intuition: Reading the review in order instead of checking which words appear.
concepts.technical: Input: integer tensor (batch, length) -> token vectors -> RNN / 1D conv / attention layers -> classifier.
concepts.significance: Replaces hand-engineered n-gram features that only capture short local order.
concepts.misconception: That sequence models automatically beat set models; the book tests this empirically in the following pages.

concepts.name: Padding and truncation
concepts.definition: Bringing variable-length sequences to a fixed length by appending [PAD] tokens or cutting off the excess.
concepts.intuition: Making all rows of a table the same width so the GPU can process them together.
concepts.technical: TextVectorization(output_sequence_length=600) zero-pads at the end and truncates at the end; index 0 is reserved for padding.
concepts.significance: Required for rectangular batches and parallel GPU computation.
concepts.example: "the slow brown badger" -> [the, slow, brown, badger, [PAD], [PAD], [PAD], [PAD]] at length 8.
concepts.misconception: That padding is harmless; the book warns that pad tokens must not affect predictions.

concepts.name: Learned features vs. engineered features
concepts.definition: Letting the model learn representations from raw input instead of designing features by hand.
concepts.intuition: Rather than listing every useful phrase, let the model discover them.
concepts.technical: n-gram features need a separate weight per phrase; sequence models share parameters across positions.
concepts.significance: A recurring deep learning principle, applied here to word order.
concepts.example: Bigrams were hand-designed features; an LSTM learns order patterns itself.
concepts.misconception: That engineered features are always worse; for small data they can be competitive, as the bigram baseline shows.

math.title: Pad-or-truncate to a fixed length
math.latex: \tilde{s}_i = \begin{cases} s_i & i \le \min(L, T) \\ \texttt{[PAD]}\ (=0) & L < i \le T \end{cases}, \qquad i = 1, \dots, T
math.source_text: Described in words: truncate input sequences or pad them with "[PAD]" to a desired length.

variables.meaning: original token sequence of length L
target length (8 in the example, 600 for IMDb)

math.operations: Keep the first T tokens; if fewer than T exist, fill the rest with the padding index.
math.purpose: Formalizes the padding/truncation rule shown in the example.
math.interpretation: Every output has exactly T positions, so a batch stacks into a (batch, T) tensor.
math.intuition: Cut long reviews, fill short ones.
math.numerical_example: T = 8. "the quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog" (L = 9) keeps 8 tokens, dropping "dog". "the slow brown badger" (L = 4) gets 8 - 4 = 4 pads.

code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: reproduce the example with TextVectorization
from keras import layers
tv = layers.TextVectorization(output_mode="int", output_sequence_length=8)
texts = ["the quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog", "the slow brown badger"]
tv.adapt(texts)
print(tv(texts))          # second row ends with four 0s
print(tv.get_vocabulary()[:2])  # ['', '[UNK]']

deeper.title: How much padding does a 600-token length imply?
deeper.body: With an average review length of 233 words, a typical sequence of 600 positions is about $233/600 \approx 39\%$ real tokens and $61\%$ padding. The 5% of reviews longer than 600 words lose their tails. This explains why almost every row in the batch on p.430 ends in zeros, and why the warning about padding affecting predictions matters. (The percentages are derived from the book's statistics; the book doesn't state them.)

deeper.title: Three ways to mix information across positions
deeper.body:
- **RNN/LSTM**: reads tokens one at a time and updates a state vector; order is built in through recurrence.
- **1D ConvNet**: learned filters over windows of k tokens, which act like soft, learned k-grams, stacked to see wider contexts.
- **Transformer**: attention lets every token look at every other token directly (next chapter).

All three take the same input: a padded integer tensor of shape (batch, length).

deeper.title: Egg cartons
deeper.body: The GPU only handles full cartons of the same size. Short reviews are filled with empty plastic eggs ([PAD]), and long reviews have extra eggs removed. The model then has to learn, or be told by masking, that the plastic eggs aren't food.

takeaways: Set models showed that word order matters, but n-gram features are hand-engineered and only capture a few words of local order.
Sequence models ingest the full token sequence and learn positional dependencies; options are RNNs, 1D ConvNets and Transformers.
Batches must be rectangular, so variable-length sequences are padded with [PAD] or truncated.
Padding speeds up batched computation, but pad tokens must not influence predictions.
IMDb reviews are truncated at 600 words (average 233; only 5% longer); index 0 is reserved for padding.

questions.question: Pad or truncate "the slow brown badger" and "the quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog" to length 8.
questions.answer: [the, slow, brown, badger, [PAD], [PAD], [PAD], [PAD]] and [the, quick, brown, fox, jumped, over, the, lazy] ("dog" is dropped).
questions.explanation: Short sequences get [PAD] tokens at the end; long ones are cut after the 8th token, as shown in the page's example.

questions.question: Why must inputs be padded or truncated to a common length?
options: Because the vocabulary has a fixed size
So batches are rectangular and computation can be parallelized across the batch on a GPU
To make reviews have the same sentiment distribution
questions.answer: So batches are rectangular and computation can be parallelized across the batch on a GPU
questions.explanation: That is the reason given on the page. Vocabulary size limits which tokens exist, not sequence length; padding doesn't remove [UNK] tokens; and sentiment distribution is unrelated.

questions.question: Why do the authors move from n-gram features to sequence models?
questions.answer: n-gram features are manually engineered and only scale to a local ordering of a few words. Deep learning prefers to expose the model to the raw sequence and let it learn positional dependencies itself.
questions.explanation: Stated at the start of 14.5, building on the intractability argument of p.428.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the sequence-model architectures listed on the page?
questions.explanation: The multi-hot linear classifier is the set model of section 14.4; the page lists RNNs, 1D ConvNets and Transformers.

questions.question: If a review has 233 tokens and sequences are padded to 600, how many [PAD] positions does it get, and what fraction of the sequence is padding?
questions.answer: 600 - 233 = 367 pad positions, about 61% of the sequence.
questions.explanation: Uses the average length of 233 quoted on the page. This much padding is why the book warns that pads must not affect predictions.

questions.question: Justify the choice of 600 as the truncation length for IMDb.
questions.answer: It keeps the input size manageable while losing little: the average review is 233 words and only 5% of reviews are longer than 600.
questions.explanation: Both statistics are given in the last paragraph.

questions.question: Can you explain the difference between [UNK] and [PAD], and why padding needs special care in a model?
questions.answer: [UNK] replaces a real word missing from the vocabulary; [PAD] is meaningless filler that equalizes lengths. Pads could distort predictions if the model treats them as content, so they need care (such as masking).
